title: Bakery Bestsellers
story: Your bakery's till logs one line per item sold: croissant, scone, croissant, bagel, and so on. The front window has room for only a few trays.
Tomorrow, today's best sellers get the window. Their ranking among themselves does not matter, only which ones make the cut.
task: Write bestsellers(sales, k). Return the k items that appear most often in sales, in any order, each item once.
The input is chosen so the answer is unique: the k-th best item always sold strictly more than the item in place k + 1.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ number of different items in sales
Item names are non-empty lowercase strings.
The set of the k most sold items is unique.

examples.explanation: Croissant sold 3, scone 2, bagel 1 and muffin 1, so the top two are croissant and scone; ["scone", "croissant"] is just as correct.
Donut sold 3, bagel 2, eclair 1. Bagel was sold first, but donut sold the most.

hints: Before you can pick the top items, what number do you need for every item? How would you get it in one pass?
Count with a map from item to count. Then pick the k biggest counts. Sorting by count works. Can you avoid a full sort?
No count can exceed sales.length. What if you made one bucket per possible count and dropped each item into its count's bucket?
Build the count map. Make buckets indexed 0 to sales.length, where bucket c holds items sold exactly c times. Walk from the highest bucket down, collecting items until you have k.
bruteForce: Count each different item by scanning the whole log, then repeatedly pick the unpicked item with the largest count.

Rescanning costs O(n) per item, so O(n · m) for m different items: hundreds of millions of steps with 100,000 sales and thousands of items. Counting once with a map and sorting the m items gives O(n + m log m), which is fine. Buckets remove even the sort.

walkthrough: Two steps: count every item in one pass with a map, then pick the biggest counts. Counts are whole numbers from 1 to n, so you can file items by count instead of sorting.
Trace [scone, croissant, bagel, croissant, scone, croissant, muffin] with k = 2:
• Buckets (0 to 7): bucket 1 = [bagel, muffin], bucket 2 = [scone], bucket 3 = [croissant], the rest empty.
• Walk down from bucket 7. Buckets 7 to 4 are empty. Bucket 3 gives croissant.
• Bucket 2 gives scone. Now there are 2 items, so stop: [croissant, scone].
Sorting the m items by count is also a good answer, and often what people write first in an interview. A heap of size k is the other common choice when k is much smaller than m.
solution.timeWhy: One pass to count, one pass over at most n buckets, and each item is placed once.
solution.spaceWhy: The count map and the n + 1 buckets.
solution.takeaway: For "most frequent" questions, count with a hash map, then select. When you rank by small integers (like counts up to n), bucketing by value replaces sorting.
